title: A future with Chinese characteristics – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Mark Leonard argues the US has lost its role as the world's image of the future to China: young people in the global south are not pro- or anti-Western but post-Western, with China — green energy, mobile payments, advanced robotics — at the centre of their imagined future. The shift is demographic and pragmatic, which also makes it shallow and reversible.

themes.theme: The aspirational centre of gravity has moved east

insights.claim: For most people in most countries the future can now be seen in China rather than the US, with China showing African, Latin American and even American young people what an economy built on green energy, mobile payments and advanced robotics looks like.
insights.so_what: Brand equity in the global south accrues to Chinese green-tech, fintech and robotics exporters — an aspirational premium Western incumbents no longer enjoy in those markets.
insights.locator: But fast-forward to 2026, and the positions have been reversed.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: Younger generations around the world are not pro- or anti-Western so much as post-Western: China, not the US, sits at the centre of their conceptual universe, which is a break from decades in which even anti-Western counter-models were defined by opposition to the West.
insights.so_what: A framework for reading emerging-market politics: alignment decisions will increasingly be made without reference to the West at all, weakening Western leverage even where hostility is absent.
insights.quote: Yet younger generations around the world are not even pro- or anti-Western so much as they are post-Western.
insights.locator: Yet younger generations around the world
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: Western disillusionment has produced “Chinamaxxing” on social media, with American and European influencers performatively adopting Chinese mannerisms and aesthetics.
insights.so_what: A cultural leading indicator that the soft-power shift is now reaching Western consumers, not just the global south.
insights.locator: In many parts of the West, disillusionment has given rise to Chinamaxxing
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: The median age is 40-50 in the US and Europe against 19 in Nigeria and 29 in South Africa, India and Lebanon, meaning around 70% of Nigerians are not old enough to have registered the 2003 Iraq invasion or the 2008 financial crisis.
insights.so_what: The demographic arithmetic explains why Western reputational capital is not recoverable through argument — the memories it rested on are absent in the median global-south voter.
insights.locator: One of the big differences between countries in the global south
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: For young West Africans the Trump era encompasses their entire political memory of the United States, and they are presumably not very impressed.
insights.so_what: US soft power in Africa is being anchored to its current worst impression rather than its historical best — a durable, generation-length handicap.
insights.quote: never knew anything more than the US as we know it now
insights.locator: As Cobus points out, young West Africans
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: In Vietnam, a country with a historically fraught relationship with China, young people are becoming less reflexively Sinophobic, with the West's perceived mishandling of covid-19 credited as the catalyst that undermined its status as a model.
insights.so_what: If attitudes are shifting even in Vietnam, the trend is stronger than country-specific grievance and should be assumed to apply broadly across Asia.
insights.locator: In Vietnam, which has long had a fraught relationship with China
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: In unstable regions such as the Middle East, much of China's attraction is its absence rather than its presence — it carries none of the colonial baggage that complicates European interventions or even peacebuilding.
insights.so_what: Chinese influence gains are partly costless and passive, which means Western “engagement” strategies can actively backfire.
insights.quote: a lot of the attraction of China is its absence rather than presence
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Loubna El Amine, a China scholar
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: The latest Arab Opinion Index shows 77% of respondents view US policies as a threat to the region's security and stability compared with just 25% for China — and that was before Trump launched his war against Iran.
insights.so_what: A hard number on the Gulf and wider Arab opinion gap, with the implication that the real figure is now worse for Washington.
insights.locator: The latest Arab Opinion Index bears this out
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

themes.theme: Why China's lead is shallower than it looks

insights.claim: China's hold on the popular imagination is tenuous because the pivot is pragmatic and non-ideological rather than a conversion to a Chinese model.
insights.so_what: Sentiment this shallow can reverse quickly on a single bad experience — do not extrapolate current Chinese brand strength in emerging markets as permanent.
insights.locator: Since the pivot to China as an exemplar of modernity
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: Chinese behaviour — predatory loans, acquiring critical national infrastructure and deliberately exporting domestic overcapacity — ruffles feathers in Thailand, Mexico and Nigeria as much as in the US and Europe.
insights.so_what: Overcapacity dumping is generating trade-defence pressure in emerging markets too, not just in the West — broader tariff risk for Chinese exporters than commonly assumed.
insights.locator: Still, China has been known to be aggressive
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: Young people's widespread distrust of their own governments can easily bleed into unhappiness with China when leaders are seen to be granting it undue privileges.
insights.so_what: Political risk for Chinese infrastructure and resource projects is transmitted through domestic anti-incumbent sentiment — watch election turnover in host countries.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: The key to winning hearts and minds is not countering Chinese propaganda or improving Western PR but offering real solutions to people's problems and creating more opportunities for prosperity.
insights.so_what: Signals that Western communications and information-operations budgets are the wrong lever; investment and market access are the ones that would work.
insights.locator: Lots of leaders in the West want to compete with China
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard

insights.claim: The reversal is historically symmetrical: China's economic reinvention was inspired in part by Deng Xiaoping's awe at American modernity during his 1979 visit, and the same aspirational pull now runs the other way.
insights.so_what: A reminder that aspirational leadership is cyclical and transferable — and that it preceded, rather than followed, China's economic catch-up.
insights.locator: China’s great economic reinvention was inspired, in part
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard
